properties.title: How Are We Safer Together?
properties.summary: In Victoria, Australia, the source describes this adaptation action: Risk-based fuel management-Used landscape-scale fire behavior modeling and community values to prioritize where and how to reduce fuels through planned burns or mechanical treatments. Community collaboration: Partnered with local governments and community members to co-design preparedness and response strategies through tailored outreach, local workshops, and shared decision-making; Behavioral insights research: Partnered with BehaviourWorks Australia to study what drives or inhibits household-level preparedness and to pilot behavior-change strategies; Smoke and health research: Collaborated with CSIRO, EPA Victoria, and BoM to assess the public health impacts of smoke and guide burn scheduling accordingly; Transparency and accountability: Developed public dashboards and reporting tools to communicate risk reduction efforts, trade-offs, and performance outcomes. Wildfire & Smoke. Project records place the work in the assess stage.

properties.title: The People and the Fire Tree: Co-Designing a Bushfire Early Warning System
properties.summary: In Victoria, Australia, the source describes this adaptation action: The project used participatory co-design methods through five workshops with residents of a rural, fire-prone community in Victoria. Participants developed two systems: The Fire Tree—a visual tool for tracking fire threat levels—and The People System—a platform integrating official government resources with informal local communication networks. The collaboration involved researchers from Swinburne University’s Centre for Design Innovation and Centre for Social Impact, emphasizing lived experience, local insight, and institutional coordination. Wildfire & Smoke, Flooding. Project records place the work in the evaluate stage. The result was Bushfire, a prototype early-warning platform tailored to local needs and designed to strengthen both formal and informal communication. The project increased residents’ sense of agency and confidence in preparedness while creating a tool that bridges gaps between community response and institutional systems. It also produced design principles that can inform similar efforts across other vulnerable regions.

properties.title: Quantifying & Visualizing Urban Heat in Portland through Community Depaving
properties.summary: In Portland, OR, the source describes this adaptation action: Remote sensing & data mapping; Collaborated with Depave, a nonprofit that engages communities in converting pavement to green spaces in vulnerable neighborhoods; Analyzed six case study locations to measure changes in LST after depaving, allowing real-world assessment of local interventions to quantify impact. Extreme Heat. Project records place the work in the adapt stage. Frontline communities identified-Mapped neighborhoods with both high temperature exposure and social vulnerability, emphasizing areas needing urgent attention; Depaving effectiveness-Demonstrated an average reduction of ~1 °F in surface temperature across depaved sites, highlighting quantifiable cooling benefits; Method development: Validated a replicable approach combining remote sensing and community intervention to assess and mitigate urban heat impacts. Washington cities like Seattle face similar challenges with urban heat and environmental inequities.

properties.title: Chicago Uses Green Infrastructure to Reduce Extreme Heat
properties.summary: In Chicago, IL, the source describes this adaptation action: Climate vulnerability assessment; Introduced green roofs, cool roofs (EPA Energy Star standards), and expanded tree canopy via incentives like expedited permits and tax-funded grants; Partnered with the Field Museum and CDC to target outreach in vulnerable, predominantly Black neighborhoods, raising awareness and building preparedness; Updated heat-response protocols, established cooling centers (e.g., libraries), expanded Notify Chicago alerts. Extreme Heat, Flooding. Project records place the work in the adapt stage. Data-driven targeting led to investments in green and cool infrastructure across the city’s heat-prone zones; Thousands of trees, cool roofs, and green roofs were installed—green roofs now feature on City Hall and commercial buildings; Heat-resilient planning was institutionalized in Chicago’s 2008 Climate Action Plan and Cook County’s Hazard Mitigation strategy; Increased community awareness and capacity to respond to heat emergencies, especially in at-risk neighborhoods.

properties.title: Adapting Paris: Climate Resilience Strategies in the Face of Rising Temperatures
properties.summary: In Paris, France, the source describes this adaptation action: Paris implemented over 1,300 “cool islands” by combining data-driven heat risk mapping with nature-based and built solutions like shaded parks, water features, and public building access. The initiative prioritized equitable access, aiming to ensure that all residents, especially in vulnerable neighborhoods, were within a 10-minute walk of a cool zone. Extreme Heat. Project records place the work in the evaluate stage. Paris successfully implemented a network of over 1,300 publicly accessible cool zones, including shaded spaces, green schoolyards, misting stations, and cooling centers; Vulnerable residents gained increased access to relief during extreme heat, reducing health risks; The initiative has become a model for other cities, demonstrating how local governments can integrate health, equity, and climate resilience into daily urban life; The strategy has been embedded in Paris’s long-term climate adaptation and public health planning.

properties.title: Paris Oasis Schoolyard Program
properties.summary: In Paris, France, the source describes this adaptation action: Through a co-design and nature-based approach Paris was able to turn heat-prone, paved schoolyards into cool, green, and accessible spaces. The project utilized community engagement strategies, climate models, and pilot projects, to successfully implement more permeable surfaces, vegetation, and water retention features to reduce urban heat and stormwater runoff within schoolyards. Extreme Heat. Project records place the work in the evaluate stage. Dozens of schoolyards across Paris were successfully redesigned and opened to the public; Surface temperatures in OASIS yards were significantly lower compared to traditional schoolyards; Increased awareness and participation among students, teachers, and neighborhood residents; The program is now being scaled up as a citywide adaptation measure. The OASIS Schoolyard Programme is highly relevant to Washington, particularly urban areas like Seattle, which experiences increased risks from extreme heat, stormwater runoff, and inequitable access to green space.

properties.title: Island County Sea Level Rise Strategy Study
properties.summary: The Island County Sea Level Rise Strategy Study aimed to enhance flood preparedness and resilience by providing an actionable framework to strengthen the county’s coastlines, infrastructure, and ecosystems in the face of rising seas. A key objective was to integrate adaptation strategies into Shoreline Master Programs and other planning documents, ensuring that technical data translated effectively into policy. The project also focused on developing practical tools, such as vulnerability maps and implementation frameworks, to support local departments in incorporating sea level rise into everyday decision-making. Through collaborative workshops and public outreach, the study grounded its recommendations in both scientific insight and community values using a co-productive approach.

properties.title: Pines on the Severn Living Shoreline
properties.summary: In Arnold, Maryland, the source describes this adaptation action: Construct a 400-foot living shoreline rather than replacing failing bulkheads with hard shoreline reinforcement. Shoreline erosion, flooding, drainage, and runoff pressures affected the community's shared Severn River waterfront. Project records place the work in the implement stage. The controlling source reports increased usable waterfront acreage, improved aesthetics and wildlife habitat, and greater resident awareness of water-quality issues. Useful as an external comparator for community shoreline planning, grant-supported implementation, and nature-based erosion control. The controlling source documents the project and source-reported observations; it does not establish independent measured effectiveness or justify broad claims about living-shoreline performance.

properties.title: Powell Shoreline Restoration Project
properties.summary: In Bainbridge Island, WA, the source describes this adaptation action: Remove bulkheads & Employ soft shoreline stabilization techniques. Marine & Coastal Changes. Project records place the work in the evaluate stage. Initiated in 2009 as a community-driven collaboration between the Powel family, Bainbridge Island Land Trust, and state and federal salmon recovery funders, the project removed approximately one-third of a mile of aging bulkheads and over 1,340 tons of riprap, concrete, and creosote timber. Over 2,500 native plants were installed, invasive species cleared, and intertidal habitat expanded by roughly 163%. A diverse stakeholder group—ranging from tribal representatives to city, engineering, and ecological experts guided the design process, supported by 1,200+ volunteer hours. The project also restored intertidal and salt marsh habitat, benefiting salmon and other wildlife. Large, private-property projects can serve as showcases and outreach opportunities, demonstrating feasibility and ecological benefits to other landowners.

properties.summary: In Seattle, WA, the source describes this adaptation action: Geo-thermal heat pumps & electric boilers. Extreme Heat and Public Health. Seattle Public Schools’ electrical supply is 91% renewable, and carbon credits offset the remaining 9%; operational greenhouse gas emissions are minimal. properties.title: San Diego Gas & Electric Wildfire Strategy
properties.summary: In San Diego, CA, the source describes this adaptation action: Through inter-organizational collaboration between SDG&E, UCLA, and the U.S. Forest Service a multidisciplinary tool was developed to aid in wildfire response and mitigation: Santa Ana Wildfire Threat Index. Wildfire & Smoke. Project records place the work in the adapt stage. Improved forecasts of fire-conducive weather, especially during Santa Ana events, with several days of advance notice. Operational enhancements, like temporarily disabling trunk lines in vulnerable areas, reducing the chance of equipment sparking fires. Cost savings, through avoided damages, reduced outages, and fewer wildfire ignitions linked to power infrastructure. Enhanced public safety, thanks to earlier alerts and better-prepared firefighters and utility staff. This case study highlights the critical role of early warning systems and localized risk forecasting, while demonstrating how public–private partnerships and collaboration with academic institutions can drive innovative, science-based solutions.

properties.title: Risks & Regulation of Invasive Plants in a Changing Climate
properties.summary: The primary goal of the Northwest RISCC Network project was to assess and address how climate change may increase the risk posed by invasive plant species in the Pacific Northwest. As temperatures rise and ecosystems shift, some non-native species that were previously benign or regionally constrained may become invasive threats. The project aimed to help land managers, policymakers, and regulatory agencies prepare for these changes by identifying high-risk species and adapting management tools and regulations accordingly.

properties.title: Natural Restoration and Cultural Knowledge of the Yakama Nation
properties.summary: This project will remove two diversion dams and a non-functional fish screen and replace them with appropriate fish passage structures on the Toppenish Creek in Washington. Removing these barriers will provide a clearer migration path to spawning habitats for Pacific lamprey and threatened steelhead. In addition to the benefits for fish species, this project will restore and enhance more than 450 acres of wetland habitat on the floodplain of Toppenish Creek. These floodplain wetlands are invaluable wildlife habitat for both migratory and resident species. Toppenish Creek is culturally significant to the Yakama Nation and the area serves as an educational site to retain tribal culture. Yakama Tribal members also hunt on the properties, and gather traditional foods and materials such as Wapato, tule, currants and chokecherries, and willow and dogwood.
